subject: history_social
passage: In 1840, Britain introduced the Penny Post, which allowed a letter to be sent anywhere in the country for a single penny, paid in advance by the sender. Within a few years, the number of letters mailed each year had more than doubled. Historian Fiona MacLeod argues that most of this increase came from working-class people writing to family and friends, many of whom had rarely been able to afford postage before the reform made it cheap. Before then, postage on a single letter traveling a long distance could equal a large part of a laborer's daily wage.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken MacLeod's argument?

choices.A: Business correspondence alone accounted for more than half of the additional letters mailed in the 1840s.
choices.B: Envelopes, which had been uncommon before 1840, came into wide use soon after the reform.
choices.C: Before 1840, postage was usually paid by the person who received a letter rather than by the sender.
choices.D: Many new post offices opened in the working-class districts of British cities during the 1840s.

explanation.why: MacLeod's claim is about where most of the new letters came from: working-class people. A finding that more than half of the additional letters were business correspondence directly contradicts that claim about the source of the increase.
explanation.A: Correct. If businesses produced most of the extra letters, working-class writers could not have produced most of them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The spread of envelopes is a change in how letters were sent, not evidence about who was sending them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This describes how postage worked before the reform but says nothing about who sent the additional letters afterward.
explanation.D: Incorrect. New post offices in working-class districts would make it easier for those people to send letters, which fits MacLeod's argument.
